subject: physiology
title: Peristalsis, the Defecation Reflex, and the Vomiting Cascade

steps.tx: The fundamental propulsive motor pattern of the gastrointestinal tract is peristalsis, governed by the classic **law of the gut**. Distension of the intestinal wall by an intraluminal bolus stimulates mucosal serotonin release, triggering contraction of circular muscle upstream and relaxation of circular muscle downstream.
steps.say: The law of the gut dictates upstream circular contraction and downstream receptive relaxation to propel food boluses.

nodes.label: Intraluminal Food Bolus Stretches Enteric Mucosa and Enterochromaffin Cells
Release of Serotonin (5-HT) Stimulates Intrinsic Primary Afferent Neurons
Ascending Interneurons Release ACh and Substance P: Upstream Circular Contraction
Descending Interneurons Release Nitric Oxide and VIP: Downstream Receptive Relaxation

steps.tx: In contrast to propulsive peristalsis, the predominant motor activity of the small intestine during active digestion is **segmental mixing contraction**. Ring-like contractions chop chyme into segments and slosh it back and forth over mucosal brush borders, maximizing nutrient contact without producing forward transit.
steps.say: Segmental contractions chop and mix chyme across the intestinal brush border without forward propulsion.

left.title: Peristaltic Propulsion
points: Coordinated upstream contraction and downstream relaxation
Travels aborally at 1 to 2 cm/sec over short distances
Primary role is forward transit of intestinal chyme
Requires intact myenteric plexus and enteric reflex arcs

right.title: Segmental Mixing
points: Isolated rhythmic contractions of circular muscle rings
Divides chyme into segments and recombines them
Maximizes nutrient contact with brush border enzymes
Governed by slow wave frequency of interstitial cells of Cajal

steps.tx: Colonic motility is characterized by slow, uncoordinated contractions that form pocket-like pouches called haustra. Approximately one to three times daily, powerful propulsive **mass movements** sweep through the transverse and descending colon, propelling faecal material rapidly into the rectum to initiate the urge to defecate.
steps.say: Mass movements occur one to three times daily, sweeping faeces into the rectum to trigger the defecation urge.

rows: Intrinsic slow waves in circular muscle
Slow kneading, desiccation, and water reabsorption
Triggered by gastrocolic and duodenocolic reflexes
Drives colonic contents into rectum in seconds
Delays emptying of caecum to maximize fluid recovery

steps.tx: Ingestion of a meal triggers prompt colonic mass contractions through the coordinated **gastrocolic reflex**. Mediated by vagovagal neural pathways and endocrine gastrin release from the gastric antrum, this physiological reflex explains the common postprandial urge to defecate, which is especially pronounced in healthy infants.
steps.say: The gastrocolic reflex stimulates colonic mass movements after meals, mediated by vagal signals and gastrin.

nodes.label: Food Ingestion Distends Stomach; Peptides Stimulate Antral Gastrin Release
Vagal Afferents Signal Brainstem; Long-Loop Vagovagal Reflex Activated
Myenteric Parasympathetic Postganglionics Stimulate Colonic Smooth Muscle
Gastrocolic Reflex Initiates Vigorous Mass Movement Toward Rectum

steps.tx: Defecation begins as a reflex the cord can run alone, then society takes over. The **intrinsic defecation reflex** uses the myenteric plexus: rectal stretch triggers peristalsis and internal sphincter relaxation, sampling contents at the anal canal. Voluntary control of the external sphincter then decides timing, the layer lost first in cord injury patterns. Understanding the two layers explains continence, megarectum and most bedside bowel programmes.
steps.say: Rectal stretch triggers an intrinsic reflex relaxing the internal sphincter, while voluntary external control decides timing. Cord injury separates the two layers.

vis.caption: Rectal stretch is shown triggering peristalsis and internal sphincter relaxation. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Faecal entry into the distensible rectal ampulla activates mechanoreceptors that trigger the **intrinsic defecation reflex**. Mediated via the myenteric plexus, peristaltic waves drive faeces through the anal canal while simultaneously relaxing the involuntary internal anal sphincter through nitric oxide release.
steps.say: Rectal distension triggers the defecation reflex, contracting rectal muscle while relaxing the internal anal sphincter.

vis.alt: Defecation reflex pathways and anorectal innervation
vis.caption: Anorectal junction reflex arcs, sphincter pressures, and autonomic regulation of continence.

steps.tx: The intrinsic reflex is reinforced by the powerful **parasympathetic defecation reflex**, transmitting sensory impulses to sacral spinal cord segments S2 through S4. Efferents travel back via pelvic splanchnic nerves, intensifying peristalsis and relaxing the internal sphincter, while continence is preserved voluntarily by the somatic pudendal nerve.
steps.say: Parasympathetic signals from sacral spinal segments reinforce defecation, while voluntary pudendal nerves control continence.

left.title: Internal Anal Sphincter
points: Tonically contracted via sympathetic hypogastric outflow
Relaxes reflexively when rectal wall is distended (rectosphincteric reflex)
Abolished in Hirschsprung disease due to missing enteric inhibitory neurons

right.title: External Anal Sphincter
points: Striated voluntary muscle encircling anal canal
Tonically active; consciously contracted to maintain continence
Can voluntarily override defecation reflex until convenient

steps.tx: The neurochemical coordination of emesis is controlled by the **brainstem vomiting center**, located in the dorsolateral reticular formation of the medulla. It integrates afferents from the chemoreceptor trigger zone, vagal gastrointestinal mechanoreceptors, vestibular nuclei in motion sickness, and higher cortical centres.
steps.say: The medullary vomiting centre integrates signals from the chemoreceptor trigger zone, vagal afferents, and vestibular system.

nodes.label: Trigger: Toxins, Chemotherapy, GI Irritation, or Vestibular Motion Sickness
Chemoreceptor Trigger Zone (Area Postrema) Senses Bloodborne Emetogens
Medullary Vomiting Center Integrates Afferents from CN VIII, IX, X, and CTZ
Coordinated Motor Surge: Retrograde Peristalsis, Diaphragm and Abdominal Contraction

steps.tx: Located in the area postrema on the floor of the fourth ventricle, the **chemoreceptor trigger zone** lacks a functional blood-brain barrier. Bathed directly by systemic arterial blood, it expresses high concentrations of dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT3 receptors, allowing circulating emetogenic toxins and chemotherapy agents to trigger vomiting.
steps.say: The chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema lacks a blood-brain barrier, sensing toxins via dopamine and serotonin receptors.
